lesson.heading: The Speaking test: 11-14 minutes, three parts
rows: Familiar topics - hobbies, likes and dislikes, daily routine
A topic from a booklet: talk for 1-2 minutes after about a minute of notes
More detailed and more abstract questions linked to the Part 2 topic
lesson.note: The examiner uses a **script**, so every Speaking test follows the same pattern. The interview is recorded.

lesson.heading: The four criteria
lesson.text: Your speaking is assessed on the same four criteria throughout the test.

examples.text: **Fluency and Coherence** - do you speak fluently and link your ideas clearly?
**Lexical Resource** - a wide range of vocabulary, used accurately? Can you explain an idea when you do not know the exact word?
**Grammatical Range and Accuracy** - a range of structures rather than the same basic ones repeated?
**Pronunciation** - clear speech, with stress and intonation that add meaning?

lesson.heading: How the test opens
lesson.text: The first exchange is always the same, so there is nothing to invent. You must bring the identification document you used when you applied.

examples.text: *Can you tell me your **full name**, please?*
*Thank you. And what **shall I call you**?*
*And can you tell me **where you're from**?*
*Can I see your **identification**, please? Thank you, OK, that's fine.*
*Now, in this first part, I'd like to ask you **some questions about yourself**.*
*Let's talk about **what you do**.* / *Let's talk about **where you live**.*

lesson.heading: Body language is part of communicating

left.label: Appropriate
examples: Making good eye contact from the moment you enter the room
Drinking from a bottle of water
Asking to leave the room for a moment if you need to
Body language that shows you are listening carefully

right.label: Not appropriate
examples: Chewing gum, even if it helps you stay calm
Checking your mobile phone, or using it to time the interview
Shrugging your shoulders instead of saying you do not understand
Asking the examiner your score at the end of the test

lesson.note: The Speaking test is a formal situation. Answer in a polite and friendly way, and look at the examiner rather than down.

lesson.heading: Never give a prepared speech
lesson.text: The test should be a natural conversation. If you try to deliver something you memorised, the examiner will interrupt you and ask a different question. Answers that are too short have the same problem in reverse - the examiner has to use the follow-up question in brackets to get any language out of you.

examples.text: *What do you like most about your home town/city?* **[Why?]**
*Is your home town/city a popular place for tourists to visit?* **[Why/Why not?]**
*Do you think your home town/city has changed much in recent years?* **[Why/Why not?]**

lesson.note: Answer the bracketed question **before** it is asked. That is what *answering fully* means.

lesson.heading: Never answer yes or no alone
lesson.text: Part 1 questions come in a variety of tenses, and a high Grammatical Range score needs you to match them and then go further. Give the short answer, then the reason.

examples.text: *Do you like to read the newspaper?* - **Yes, I do.** / **Not really.**
*Did you enjoy studying when you first started school?* - **Yes, I did.** / **No, I didn't.**
*Would you like to do any further study?* - **Yes, I would.** / **No, I wouldn't.**
*Have you always liked the same kind of music?* - **Yes, I have.** / **No, I haven't.**
*Are there any special festivals in your city?* - **Yes, there is.** / **No, there aren't.**

lesson.note: Then add the detail: *Not actually* is an error for *Not really*, and *I think less, because technology nowadays are really go fast* needs *is going* - accuracy counts as much as range.

lesson.text: Record yourself answering these questions, then write out what you said. Spoken language gives you less thinking time, so the mistakes you make when speaking are different from the ones you make when writing - and you cannot fix them until you can see them.

exercises.prompt: What must you bring to the Speaking test?
options: The identification document you used when you applied
A copy of your practice answers
exercises.explanation: *Can I see your identification, please?* comes near the start of the examiner's script. Paper and a pencil are provided for Part 2.

exercises.statement: Learning a prepared speech is a good way to sound fluent in Part 1.
exercises.explanation: The test should be a natural conversation. If you give a prepared speech the examiner will interrupt and ask something else.

exercises.prompt: Match each question with its short answer.

pairs.left: Did you enjoy studying at school?
Would you like to do any further study?
Have you always liked the same music?
Do you like to read the newspaper?
Are there any festivals in your city?

exercises.prompt: Correct the error: *I think less, because technology nowadays ___ really fast.* (go)
exercises.explanation: *Technology* is uncountable and singular, and the sentence describes a change in progress - so *is going*, not *are go*.

exercises.prompt: Why does the examiner put a follow-up question in brackets, such as *[Why?]*
options: It is a harder question you may skip
It is used when your answer was too short to assess
It is always asked, in every test
It is a question you ask the examiner
exercises.explanation: Answer it before it is asked and your answer is already full - which is what the criteria reward.

exercises.prompt: Build the examiner's first question in the test.
exercises.answer: Can you tell me your full name, please?
exercises.explanation: The opening of the script is fixed, so there is nothing to prepare - just answer it clearly.

exercises.prompt: Match each criterion with what the examiner is listening for.

pairs.right: speaking easily and linking ideas clearly
a wide range of vocabulary, used accurately
varied structures rather than the same basic ones
clear speech, with stress and intonation that add meaning

exercises.statement: Shrugging your shoulders is an acceptable way to show you did not understand a question.
exercises.explanation: Say so instead - *I'm not really sure what you mean* or *Could you repeat the question?* Silence and gestures give the examiner no language to assess.
